title: Siblings
hook: Jacob and Esau, Martha and Mary: sibling love takes work
tomorrow: what's the difference between a friend and a teammate?

segments.voice: Yesterday, parents: honor, honestly, like the twelve-year-old who told the truth and still went home with them. Today, the ones who grew up at the same table.

A sibling group chat: one sends a photo, another leaves it on read, and an argument about the front seat from age nine is somehow still running. Why do brothers in the Bible fight so much? Cain and Abel. Joseph sold by his brothers. Jacob and Esau. Even Martha, stuck in the kitchen, asking Jesus to make her sister help. The Bible doesn't hide it. Sibling love, it seems, takes work.
screen: `LEFT ON READ.` → `THE BIBLE DOESN'T HIDE IT.` → `SIBLING LOVE TAKES WORK.`

segments.voice: Take the hardest case. Jacob tricks his twin Esau out of their father's blessing and runs for his life. Years later he has to come home, and he's terrified. He sends gifts ahead and bows low as his brother approaches. And Genesis says Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept. Some readers hear that run again in Luke, when the father runs to the son who wasted everything. The answer here: sibling love isn't the love you're born with. It's the long walk back, and someone willing to run. Martha's version is smaller and closer to home: Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Jesus answers her by name, twice, gently, and doesn't take sides in the way she hoped. Now a neighbor's reading of the same story. Jews read Jacob and Esau in the Torah, and the commentator Rashi notes that the word kissed has dots written over it in the scroll. He records two readings. Some say Esau didn't kiss him with his whole heart. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says that at that moment Esau's compassion was stirred, and he kissed him with all his heart. Here's what's shared: both traditions keep this embrace as a picture of brothers coming home. And here's an honest difference. Jewish readers weigh the kiss through the rabbis' debate. Catholic readers can hear it alongside the Gospel's running father. Two homes for one old story, ranking neither.
screen: `ESAU RAN TO MEET HIM.` · `MARTHA, MARTHA.` · `RASHI: DOTS OVER THE KISS.` · `ONE STORY, TWO HOMES.` · then, large: `BROTHERS AND SISTERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a brother or sister, by birth or by choice, the easy one or the hard one. Open a message to them and type one plain line, the kind that runs toward them a little. Send it now, later, or not at all; just sit with the line on the screen.
Siblings. The ones who share your table and your old fights, and the long walk back. Today's word.
Pocket this one: brothers and sisters, the kind someone has to run toward. Until tomorrow.

chat.meaning: The Bible doesn't hide sibling fights. Jacob and Esau were apart for years, and the story still ends in an embrace. It takes work, and time.

Martha.meaning: Mary's sister, who served while Mary listened to Jesus

Torah.meaning: the five books of Moses, read in the synagogue

Rashi.meaning: a Jewish commentator on the Torah and Talmud

Shimon bar Yochai.meaning: a rabbi quoted in Rashi and other Jewish texts
